hints: Look at the carbon in carvone that carries the $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$ group and check how many different groups are attached to it.
walkthrough:
Spot what makes optical isomerism possible**
Picture a carbon with four completely different arms. It has no mirror plane through it, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed. That is exactly what we call a chiral centre, and it is the key to optical isomerism.

Apply this to carvone**
Look at the ring carbon joined to the $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$ side chain. It is joined to H, to that alkenyl side chain, and to two different directions round the unsymmetrical ring (one side toward $\text{C}=\text{O}$, one side toward $\text{C}=\text{C}$). Four different groups means it is chiral, so carvone exists as two non-superimposable mirror images, the spearmint and caraway forms.
Final answer: Optical isomerism, as carvone contains a chiral carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

hints: Count carbons, hydrogens and oxygens in carvone and in X from the displayed structures to get $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ and $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$.
Compare H counts to work out how many $\text{H}_2$ molecules must add when two $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bonds and one $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond are reduced.
walkthrough:
Get the two molecular formulae**
Count carefully. Carvone has 10 carbons, 14 hydrogens and one oxygen, so $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$. Product X is fully saturated in the side chain and ring except the ring itself, with a secondary alcohol, giving $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$. Oxygen is unchanged.

Balance the hydrogen**
X has 6 more H atoms than carvone. Each $\text{H}_2$ supplies 2 H, so you need 3 $\text{H}_2$. Chemically this is one $\text{H}_2$ for the ring $\text{C}=\text{C}$, one for the side chain $\text{C}=\text{C}$, and one for reduction of $\text{C}=\text{O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$. That gives $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2 \longrightarrow \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall what happens when an alkyl group replaces a H on a benzene ring in the presence of a halogen carrier.
walkthrough:
Recognise the transformation**
You start with methylbenzene and you put an isopropyl, $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, group onto the ring para to the methyl. A H on the ring is replaced by a carbon electrophile while the aromatic ring is retained. That family is electrophilic substitution, in this case Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
Final answer: Electrophilic substitution (Friedel-Crafts alkylation).

hints: Look at step 3 where $\text{NO}_2$ becomes $\text{NH}_2$ and think about gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
Look at step 5 where $\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ becomes $\text{OH}$ and think about replacement of the diazo group by a nucleophile.
walkthrough:
Classify step 3**
$\text{Ar-NO}_2$ changes to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$. Nitrogen goes from a highly oxidised state to a reduced amine. Oxygen is lost and hydrogen is gained, so this is reduction.

Classify step 5**
$\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ changes to $\text{Ar-OH}$. The diazonium group $\text{N}_2^+$ leaves as $\text{N}_2$ and is replaced by $\text{OH}$ from water. That is nucleophilic substitution, often called hydrolysis of the diazonium salt.

Final answer: step 3: reduction
step 5: substitution / hydrolysis

hints: For step 1 think which chloroalkane supplies the $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$ group and which Lewis acid generates the carbocation.
For step 2 recall the two concentrated acids that generate the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile for nitration.
For step 3 recall the metal plus concentrated acid that reduces $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ in non-alkaline conditions.
For step 4 recall the nitrous acid system made in situ at low temperature to form a diazonium salt.
Recall why nitration must be kept below about $55^\circ\text{C}$ and diazotisation kept in ice.
Check that each step specifies both reagent and correct low temperature where required.
walkthrough:
Build the isopropyl electrophile in step 1**
You need to add $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ para to methyl. Use 2-chloropropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$, with a halogen carrier such as anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$. The catalyst polarises the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to give the $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ electrophile for Friedel-Crafts alkylation. $\text{FeCl}_3$, $\text{AlBr}_3$ or $\text{FeBr}_3$ are equivalent.

Nitrate in step 2**
The next group is $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to methyl. The classic nitrating mixture is concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, which forms $\text{NO}_2^+$. Keep $T < 55^\circ\text{C}$ to ensure mononitration and to avoid oxidation or dinitration. Directing effects of methyl and isopropyl both favour the observed position.

Reduce nitro to amine in step 3**
Convert $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, $\text{Sn}$ + $\text{HCl}$, with heating. This is the standard acidic reduction. It first gives the phenylammonium salt, then alkali liberates the free amine.

Diazotise in step 4**
Convert the primary aromatic amine to the diazonium salt with nitrous acid, made in situ from $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$. The key condition is $T < 10^\circ\text{C}$, usually 0 to $5^\circ\text{C}$ in an ice bath, because the diazonium ion decomposes to phenol and nitrogen if warmed.

Final answer: step 1: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$ (or $\text{AlBr}_3$ / $\text{FeCl}_3$ / $\text{FeBr}_3$)
step 2: conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $T < 55^\circ\text{C}$
step 3: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$ (heat, then $\text{NaOH}$ to liberate amine)
step 4: $\text{HNO}_2$ or $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$, $T < 10^\circ\text{C}$ (ice bath)

hints: Recall what reagent combination saturates a benzene ring to a cyclohexane ring.
walkthrough:
Force hydrogen onto the stable ring**
A benzene ring is very resistant because of its delocalised pi system. To add three moles of $\text{H}_2$ across it you need hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst under vigorous conditions, heat and high pressure. This is catalytic hydrogenation, the same type of process as carvone to X.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2$ with Ni catalyst, with heat and high pressure.

hints: Place $\text{CH}_3$ at the top, $\text{OH}$ ortho to it, and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ para to $\text{CH}_3$ on the cyclohexane skeleton.
Think what same side addition means for the six new H atoms and therefore for the relative positions of the three substituents.
walkthrough:
Draw the correct connectivity**
Keep the same carbon skeleton as X. Put $\text{CH}_3$ at the top carbon, $\text{OH}$ on the adjacent carbon to the right, and the isopropyl group $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$ on the bottom carbon para to the methyl. That matches the phenol precursor.

Make the addition all cis**
The benzene ring is flat. If all six H atoms attack from the same face, say from above, they all end up on the same side of the new cyclohexane ring. That forces the three existing groups, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, to all be pushed to the opposite face together. So show the H atoms on C1, C2 and C4 all as wedges (or all as dashes) and the three substituents all cis to each other. This is the most likely single diastereomer.

Final answer: Structure of X skeleton with $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ on the correct ring carbons (1,2,4 positions) with all three substituents cis to each other, i.e. all ring H atoms on C1, C2 and C4 on the same face (all wedged or all dashed).
